summary.summary: Cover report for Sandwell's draft 2025/26 Statement of Accounts, published on the council website on 30 June 2026 in line with the statutory deadline; Grant Thornton began fieldwork on 13 July 2026, targeting audit completion by 10 November and final publication by 30 November 2026, well inside the 31 January 2027 backstop. The draft CIES reports net income of £109.6m, with General Fund balances up £10.6m, HRA balances down £1.1m and capital-programme reserves up £15.8m — a strengthening usable-reserves position. One open item: a specialist adviser is reviewing all four PFI financial models for consistency and compliance, and the council cannot yet quantify what adjustments that review will feed into the final accounts. Group accounts consolidate the wholly-owned Sandwell Children's Trust.

signals.headline: Draft 2025/26 accounts published 30 June 2026 on the statutory deadline; General Fund balances improved £10.6m, but a review of four PFI financial models is ongoing with the impact not yet quantifiable
signals.why: The reserves direction is positive for creditors, but the PFI model review is an open-ended adjustment risk sitting in the draft until the November 2026 audit completion.

news_drafts.headline: Sandwell forecasts £34.7m schools grant overspend for 2026/27, all of it in high needs
news_drafts.lead:
Sandwell Council forecasts a £34.7m overspend for 2026/27 on its dedicated schools grant, the government grant that funds schools. All of it is in high needs, the part of school funding for children with special educational needs and disabilities (SEND). The draft medium-term financial strategy puts the cumulative high needs deficit at £40.753m at year-end, up from £6.053m, and says demand for SEND services has risen beyond budgeted levels.

The government has announced it intends to fund 90% of high needs deficits built up to the end of 2025/26. The council assumes £5.448m, subject to Department for Education approval of a local SEND Reform Plan. If it is received, the year-end deficit would be £35.305m. The papers say the council will be reliant on government providing additional high needs funding in the current and future years. They say the 90% is not confirmed for 2026/27 and 2027/28.

A statutory override, a temporary government rule that keeps the deficit off the main balance sheet, runs to March 2028. The papers estimate around 10% of the cumulative deficit at that date is likely to become a charge to the General Fund, the council's main account for day-to-day spending. The cabinet report also gives a forecast budget pressure of £7.7m in 2027/28 on SEND home to school transport, because of rising numbers of children with education, health and care plans. It proposes £7.7m of ongoing growth for it.
news_drafts.paper_title: Appendix 2 - Draft Medium-Term Financial Strategy 2027/28 to 2031/32

news_drafts.headline: Sandwell forecasts a £34.7m high needs overspend for 2026/27, taking the schools deficit to £40.753m
news_drafts.lead:
Sandwell Council forecasts that the high needs block, the part of school funding for children with special educational needs and disabilities (SEND), will overspend by £34.7m in 2026/27. That would take the cumulative deficit on the dedicated schools grant (DSG), the government grant that funds schools, from £6.053m to £40.753m at the end of the year. The figures are in the draft medium-term financial strategy, the council's plan for the next five years, for the Budget and Corporate Scrutiny Management Board meeting on 3 November 2026.

The paper attributes the overspend to demand for SEND services beyond budgeted levels. It says the government intends to fund 90% of high needs deficits to the end of 2025/26 through a High Needs Stability Grant, subject to a Department for Education-approved SEND Reform Plan, and that the council will rely on similar arrangements for 2026/27. On that basis £5.448m is assumed fundable, which would leave a year-end deficit of £35.305m. Accounting rules keep the deficit off the council's main General Fund until March 2028. The paper says around 10% of the cumulative deficit at that date is likely to become a charge to the General Fund.

SEND home-to-school transport has a forecast budget pressure of £7.7m in 2027/28, which the papers link to more children with education, health and care plans and to transport market inflation. The draft budget shows the pressure at £25.9m by 2031/32. Savings from cost mitigations and efficiencies within the service are set at £1.5m in 2027/28, rising to £8.996m by 2031/32. The strategy proposes £7.7m of ongoing growth in the children and education budget.
news_drafts.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Medium-Term Financial Strategy - Autumn 2026 Update (Cabinet Report)

news_drafts.headline: Sandwell forecasts £34.7m high needs overspend in 2026/27, taking cumulative deficit to £40.753m
news_drafts.lead:
Sandwell Council's draft medium-term financial strategy forecasts an overspend of £34.700m in 2026/27 on high needs, the part of the dedicated schools grant that funds support for children with special educational needs and disabilities. The cumulative high needs deficit was £6.053m before this year. It is forecast to reach £40.753m by the end of 2026/27.

A statutory override, a temporary government rule that keeps a schools-funding deficit off the main balance sheet, prevents the deficit being charged to the council's General Fund reserves until March 2028. The strategy assumes £5.448m, 90% of the cumulative deficit to the end of 2025/26, will be met by a government High Needs Stability Grant, subject to Department for Education approval of a SEND Reform Plan. That leaves £35.305m. The autumn update says the government is likely to fund 90% of deficits, and that around 10% of the council's cumulative high needs deficit at the end of March 2028 is likely to become a General Fund charge from April 2028.

Separately, home to school transport for pupils with special educational needs is forecast to face a budget pressure of £7.7m in 2027/28. The paper links this to a rising number of children with education, health and care plans, and proposes £7.7m of ongoing growth in the Children and Education budget.
news_drafts.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Medium-Term Financial Strategy - Autumn 2026 Update (Cabinet Report)

findings.committee: Budget and Corporate Scrutiny Management Board
findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 - Draft Medium-Term Financial Strategy 2027/28 to 2031/32
findings.headline: EHCP numbers in Sandwell forecast to grow from approximately 5,000 in 2025/26 to 9,500 or more by 2031/32
findings.detail: The paper says the EHCP cohort has grown by around 30% over the last year. It forecasts that around 33% of additional children will be eligible for home to school transport, creating a General Fund pressure of £7.7m in 2027/28.
findings.matters: EHCP growth drives both the High Needs deficit and the General Fund transport pressure, so it is the common root of the two largest SEND-related exposures in the paper.
findings.figures: approximately 5,000 EHCPs in 2025/26 to 9,500 or more by 2031/32; around 30% growth in the last year; 33% of additional children forecast eligible for transport; £7.7m SEND transport pressure in 2027/28
findings.quote: The number of children with EHCPs could grow from approximately 5,000 in 2025/26 to 9,500 or more by 2031/32.

findings.committee: Budget and Corporate Scrutiny Management Board
findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 - Draft Medium-Term Financial Strategy 2027/28 to 2031/32
findings.headline: HRA reserves are forecast to fall below the required level around year 20 of the 30-year Business Plan, with the HRA moving into deficit by year 24
findings.detail: The paper says rent convergence and lower borrowing costs keep the HRA stable in the short term, but reliance on borrowing to fund investment in existing homes causes debt and interest costs to rise over time. A regional benchmark of £67,000 per property has been added for capital expenditure, a rise of £25,000.
findings.matters: A ringfenced housing account that does not balance over its 30-year plan, and depends on borrowing, is a risk other councils with large HRA stock are also modelling.
findings.figures: £67,000 per property capital benchmark, up £25,000; reserves below required level around year 20; HRA in deficit by year 24; £8.9m 2026/27 HRA reserve draw
findings.quote: This demonstrates that the HRA is currently not sustainable over the 30- year timeframe without further cost reduction measures

findings.committee: Budget and Corporate Scrutiny Management Board
findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 - Draft Medium-Term Financial Strategy 2027/28 to 2031/32
findings.headline: Employer pension contribution rate falls to 17.4% for the current three-year period from 24.6%, with 19.1% projected for the final two years of the MTFP
findings.detail: The paper says the rate is set by the triennial West Midlands Pension Fund valuation and that the outcome of the next valuation, due after 2028/29, is uncertain. The increase to 19.1% is a projection for the final two years of the MTFP.
findings.matters: The change in employer contribution rates moves the pay bill by a material amount, and councils in the same fund will face the same valuation outcome.
findings.figures: 17.4% contribution rate for the current three-year period; 24.6% for the period up to 2025/26; 19.1% projected for final two years of the MTFP; 3.6% per annum pay increase assumed
findings.quote: Therefore, contribution rates for the final two years of the MTFP are projected to increase to 19.1%.

findings.committee: Budget and Corporate Scrutiny Management Board
findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 - Draft Medium-Term Financial Strategy 2027/28 to 2031/32
findings.headline: One-off £1.3m draw from earmarked reserves funded by Birmingham Airport dividends in 2026/27 is used to balance the 2027/28 budget
findings.detail: The paper says the council does not budget for airport dividends because timing and value are uncertain, so the windfall is treated as a one-year addition. It says the approach repeats the 2026/27 draft budget.
findings.matters: Using one-off dividend receipts to balance a recurring budget is a choice finance directors and lenders look at when judging whether a balance is structural.
findings.figures: £1.3m one-off draw in 2027/28; nil in 2028/29 to 2031/32
findings.quote: This would result in a draw from reserves of £1.3m in 2027/28 in order to help to balance the budget.

findings.committee: Budget and Corporate Scrutiny Management Board
findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 - Draft Medium-Term Financial Strategy 2027/28 to 2031/32
findings.headline: Draft revenue borrowing cost budget for 2027/28 is reduced to £23.8m, a £2.1m cut that leaves £3.9m of headroom for further project requests
findings.detail: The paper says the reduction is used to help balance the 2027/28 budget. It says borrowing costs remain within the council's 6% cap on net budget, and that surpluses or deficits on borrowing costs will move in or out of a Capital Financing earmarked reserve.
findings.matters: A one-off cut to the borrowing budget is a choice to draw on future capacity, and a lender or finance director will read the 6% cap and the headroom as the measures of how much further prudential borrowing the council can absorb.
findings.figures: £23.8m revised 2027/28 borrowing budget; £2.1m reduction; £3.9m headroom; 5.0% of net revenue budget in 2027/28; 5.4% in later years; 6% cap
findings.quote: it is possible to reduce the draft revenue budget for borrowing costs to £23.8m

daily_post.headline: Prudential borrowing headroom temporarily reduced to 5% of net revenue budget for 2027/28 only (down from standard 6% limit) to release £2.1m to help balance the budget.
daily_post.lead: Reducing prudential borrowing headroom, even temporarily, signals constrained debt capacity; lenders track headroom availability as an indicator of financial flexibility and the council's ability to fund future capital investment.
